summary: This Wikipedia-derived note describes the Russian language's history from Kievan Rus' onward, its official or minority status and speaker numbers in Armenia and Georgia, and its spread through Eastern Europe, North America and the former Soviet states. It also covers dialect features, the decline of Russian speaking in some regions, and its relationship to Ukrainian, Belarusian, Rusyn and Bulgarian.
one_line: Overview of the Russian language's history, status in neighbouring countries, diaspora communities, dialects and relationship to other East Slavic languages.
key_facts: The political unification of the East Slavic region into Kievan Rus' in about 880 established Old East Slavic as a literary and commercial language.
Christianity was adopted in 988, and the South Slavic Old Church Slavonic was introduced as the liturgical and official language.
In Armenia, Russian has no official status but is recognised as a minority language under the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities.
According to Demoskop Weekly estimates, in 2004 there were 15,000 native speakers of Russian in Armenia and 1 million active speakers.
In Georgia, Demoskop Weekly estimated 130,000 native speakers of Russian in 2004 and 1.7 million active speakers.
Russian is the language of 9% of Georgia's population according to the World Factbook, and Ethnologue cites Russian as the country's de facto working language.
Russian explorers first introduced the language to North America when they voyaged into Alaska and claimed it for Russia during the 1700s.
Most Russian colonists left Alaska after the United States bought the land in 1867, but a handful stayed and preserved the language there.
According to the United States Census, in 2007 Russian was the primary language spoken in the homes of over 850,000 individuals in the United States.
Only about 25% of Russian speakers in North America are ethnic Russians.
Before the dissolution of the Soviet Union, most Russophones in Brighton Beach, Brooklyn were Russian-speaking Jews.
According to the Eurobarometer 2005 survey, fluency in Russian remains fairly high (20–40%) in Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Bulgaria.
Russian was declared the official language of the Soviet Union only in 1990, though it held a unifying and superior status during the Soviet period.
Surzhyk in eastern Ukraine and Trasianka in Belarus are language mixtures that arose from traditional bilingualism with Russian's East Slavic relatives.
In the 19th century the language was often called 'Great Russian' to distinguish it from Belarusian, then called 'White Russian', and Ukrainian, then called 'Little Russian'.

entities.name: Kievan Rus'
entities.role: Political entity formed by unification of the East Slavic region in about 880, from which modern Russia, Ukraine and Belarus trace their origins

entities.name: Old Church Slavonic
entities.role: South Slavic language introduced as the liturgical and official language after the adoption of Christianity in 988

entities.name: Demoskop Weekly
entities.role: Journal whose estimates of Russian speakers in Armenia and Georgia and whose 2006 publication on Russian's declining position are cited

entities.name: Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities
entities.role: Convention under which Russian is recognised as a minority language in Armenia and Georgia

entities.name: World Factbook
entities.role: Source cited for a 2009 estimate of 1.4% Russian speakers in Armenia and a figure of 9% in Georgia

entities.name: Ethnologue
entities.role: Source citing Russian as the de facto working language of Georgia

entities.name: Eurobarometer 2005
entities.role: Survey reporting fluency in Russian of 20–40% in Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Bulgaria

entities.name: Alaska
entities.role: Territory where Russian explorers introduced the language in the 1700s and where a few elderly speakers of a unique dialect remain

entities.name: United States
entities.role: Country that bought Alaska in 1867 and has large Russian-speaking communities; the 2007 Census counted over 850,000 Russian-speaking households members

entities.name: Brighton Beach
entities.role: Brooklyn neighbourhood where most Russophones before the Soviet dissolution were Russian-speaking Jews

entities.name: Soviet Union
entities.role: State whose break-up in 1991 led several newly independent states to encourage their native languages; its government established compulsory education that forced out peasant dialects

entities.name: Surzhyk
entities.role: Language mixture arising from traditional bilingualism in eastern Ukraine

entities.name: Trasianka
entities.role: Language mixture arising from traditional bilingualism in Belarus

entities.name: Arefyev A. L.
entities.role: Research deputy director at the Research Center for Sociological Research of the Ministry of Education and Science (Russia) who concluded Russian is gradually losing its position worldwide
